# A4 — What predicts disclosed pay, and who discloses? (short form)

*Draft, 2026-10-18. Generated by `python -m analysis.a4_disclosure`; numbers in
`report/a4_results.json`. Salary fields come from `extraction/salary.py`.*

## Answer

**Almost nobody discloses, and who does is decided at the employer level, not per posting.**
3.8% of postings show an India pay range (22 of 586; 95% CI 2.5–5.6%), and **all 22 are Airbnb**.
Among technical IC postings the rate is 2.2% (6 of 270). No other employer shows an India range on
any posting. The plan's two A4 models, a log-salary regression and a selection model for
disclosure, **can't be estimated on this panel**, and pretending otherwise would produce precise-
looking numbers about one company. The one estimable finding is inside that company: **Airbnb
discloses pay for 19 of 20 non-engineering roles but only 3 of 9 engineering roles** (Fisher exact
p = 0.001).

## What counts as disclosure

| Source | What's there | Counted? |
|---|---|---|
| Airbnb descriptions | "India Annual Pay Range ₹1,960,000 — ₹2,800,000 INR" on 22 of 29 postings | **Yes** |
| GitLab descriptions | US-only ranges ("for residents of the United States only") on 2 postings | No: says nothing about India pay |
| Okta / MongoDB ATS custom fields | "Minimum Salary", "Job Post Range (United States)", "Baseline Budgeted Salary (INR)" on every posting, **all placeholder values** (0.0 or USD 0.01) | No: a zero means not disclosed, never a salary of zero |
| Ashby compensation block | Empty for every Ashby posting | No |

The MongoDB fields are worth a sentence in the report. The employer tracks an INR budget per
requisition in its ATS; the field just isn't published.

| Employer | Postings | India range shown | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|
| Okta | 190 | 0 | 0–2% |
| MongoDB | 119 | 0 | 0–3% |
| Stripe | 67 | 0 | 0–5% |
| GitLab | 65 | 0 | 0–6% |
| Twilio | 37 | 0 | 0–9% |
| Elastic | 32 | 0 | 0–11% |
| **Airbnb** | **29** | **22 (76%)** | 58–88% |
| OpenAI | 15 | 0 | 0–20% |
| Others (Datadog, Cursor, Postman, Cloudflare, Deepgram) | 32 | 0 | — |

## Why the plan's models aren't estimable

- **Part one, the log-salary regression,** would run on 22 postings from one employer. With standard
  errors clustered by company, as the plan rightly requires, there is a single cluster, so the
  standard errors don't exist. Without clustering, 22 postings sharing one pay policy would give
  intervals that are far too narrow.
- **Part two, the disclosure model,** would predict disclosure from company size, seniority, family
  and so on. Company alone separates disclosure perfectly outside Airbnb, so the model would learn
  "is it Airbnb" and nothing else. A Heckman correction needs variation in disclosure that some
  variable shifts independently of pay; there is none to work with.
- **So the selection problem is total rather than partial.** We know nothing about pay at the 95%
  of postings that make up most of the market, and nothing in this panel can tell us how Airbnb's
  pay compares to theirs.

## Within Airbnb: engineering withholds

| | Disclosed | Not disclosed |
|---|---|---|
| Engineering roles (SWE, SRE/infra, data eng, ML, QA) | 3 | 6 |
| Other roles (analytics, operations, support, product, management) | 19 | 1 |

Fisher exact p = 0.001. The six non-disclosing engineering postings include Staff SWE, Senior Staff
SWE (Payments), Engineering Manager, Tech Lead Manager (Oracle ERP), Senior Data Engineer and
Operations Engineer, mostly in "Tech Foundations" and "BizTech". This could be team-level posting
templates rather than a deliberate choice; the panel can't tell which. With n = 29 at one company,
it's an observation worth reporting, not a general claim about engineering pay transparency.

**What the disclosed ranges look like** (descriptive only): midpoints run from ₹5.4 L/yr (Support
Specialist) to ₹68 L/yr (Staff Platform Manager). The one SWE range is ₹30.5–43.5 L, and the
Senior SWE (AI/ML) range is ₹45–65 L. Ranges are wide: the top is a median 43% above the bottom.

## What this means for the rest of the report

- **Salary disclosure can't be an A2 covariate** as the plan suggests. It's collinear with Airbnb,
  which the within-company Cox model already absorbs.
- **The panel can't speak to pay levels.** Any statement about Indian tech pay from this data would
  describe one employer's posted bands.
- **This is still a result:** among global tech companies hiring in India, voluntary pay
  transparency is close to zero, and where it exists it is a company policy with exceptions, not a
  market norm.

## Reproduce

```bash
python -m extraction.salary        # writes salary_* columns (also run by `python -m extraction`)
python -m analysis.a4_disclosure
```
